title: Model-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Quantum Networks
authors: Amal Elsokary, Hayato Ishida, Ran Wei, Michael J. de C. Henshaw, Siyuan Ji
abstract: Quantum networks are advancing towards larger and more operational infrastructures, yet their evaluation remains fragmented across heterogeneous physical platforms, simulators, protocols, and architectural abstractions. Current digital-twin studies for quantum networks mainly realise isolated capabilities or application-specific solutions rather than reusable system-level twins. This paper argues that Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) can provide a systematic basis for integrating and evolving these heterogeneous artefacts. It derives requirements for design-time evaluation and runtime synchronisation, and proposes a progression of architectures from code-driven and domain-model-driven solutions to point-to-point and hub-and-spoke integration. A conceptual implementation case study illustrates this using SysML v2, QKD kit, an EMF-based controller, and SeQUeNCe. The work provides a foundation for adaptable and interoperable digital twins for quantum networks.
summary: This paper proposes a Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) framework to overcome the fragmentation in evaluating large-scale Quantum Networks. It establishes a systematic approach for building digital twins that integrate diverse components—from system models (SysML v2) to physical hardware kits and simulators. The resulting framework allows for rigorous, traceable testing of network performance across design and runtime phases.
main_problem: Evaluating quantum networks is difficult due to fragmentation across heterogeneous platforms, simulators, and abstractions, leading to isolated digital twin studies.
main_result: The paper proposes a Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) framework that provides a systematic basis for creating adaptable and interoperable system-level digital twins for quantum networks.
method: It derives requirements for design-time evaluation and runtime synchronization, proposing an architectural progression from code-driven to hub-and-spoke integration using MDE principles.
model_or_system: The focus is on Quantum Networks (QNs) and their digital twin representation. The framework uses SysML v2 as a 'hub model' to integrate physical QKD kits, simulators, and control logic.
key_observables: System-level performance metrics such as throughput, keyRate, latency, and errorRate are used for comparison between predicted (simulated) and observed (physical) behavior.
important_parameters: Quantum channel distance ($d$), maximum allowed error rate ($	ext{maxAllowedErrorRate}$), and network configuration parameters.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that MDE can systematically manage the complexity arising from integrating diverse, heterogeneous quantum simulation tools and physical hardware interfaces.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the layered structure of QNs and the conceptualization of a Digital Twin (Actual System $\leftrightarrow$ Virtual Mirror $\leftrightarrow$ Services). A key figure shows the hub-and-spoke architecture mapping to a BB84 feasibility implementation.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the fragmentation problem, then introduces MDE as the solution foundation. It details the two operational loops (design-time/runtime) and progresses through four architectural levels of integration complexity before demonstrating a proof-of-concept using SysML v2 for QKD.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it addresses the crucial engineering challenge of validating complex quantum hardware systems by providing a formal, model-driven methodology to link theory/simulation with physical realization.

Figure 1 presents one layered perspective of a quantum net- work, comprising physical infrastructure, device-control functions, network-control functions, and quantum-network applications. It illustrates how application-level capabilities, including QKD, quan- tum teleportation, and end-to-end entanglement distribution, de- pend on the coordinated operation of devices, protocols, and control functions across interconnected layers. Although the layers organisation and terminology may differ across architectural proposals, the figure demonstrates that the operation and performance of each layer depend on functions, resources, and information exchanged across other layers.
